reading.rtitle: What to Say, and What to Leave Out
paras: Every year, thousands of researchers arrive at a congress with twenty minutes and ten years of work. The ones people remember are not the ones with the most data. They are the ones who decided, before the trip, what to leave out. One senior researcher puts it in one line: choose one result, and build everything around it. A presenter who refuses to cut anything loses the room after four minutes.

The same choice happens in conversation. Experienced presenters avoid starting with the method. They start with the question, because that is what a stranger can follow. They also keep checking the room, and when somebody looks confused, they stop and ask. Many people consider stopping a sign of weakness. It is the opposite: the presenters who never stop are the ones who lose the audience.

And the questions at the end? Most presenters expect to answer questions about the method, not only about the results, so they prepare two or three short answers before the session. If you do not understand a question, ask the person to repeat it. Nobody manages to catch every accent in a room with forty countries in it. Experienced researchers recommend saying so out loud, in one short sentence, and then going on.
reading.source: Adapted for this class from advice given to first-time presenters at international congresses.

listenings.text: Let me tell you how I plan a congress day, because my first congress was a disaster. I tried to attend everything, and at six o'clock in the evening I remembered nothing. Now I do the opposite. The night before, I read the program and I decide on three sessions. Three, not ten. I avoid choosing two talks in the same hour, because then I spend the hour walking between rooms. And I always keep one hour free in the afternoon, for the corridor. The corridor is where the real work happens. People ask me if I miss good talks. Of course I do. But I manage to have three real conversations, and in December I still remember all of them.

I have two recommendations for anybody standing at a poster for the first time. First, do not read your own poster to people. They can read. Instead, ask them one question: what brings you to this topic? Then you know what to say and what to leave out. Second, I recommend preparing three versions of your work: thirty seconds, two minutes, and ten minutes. You decide which one to use after the first question, never before it. And there is one thing I avoid completely: apologizing for my English. Nobody in that room is thinking about your grammar. They are thinking about your data. Keep talking, and they will stay.
